name: Smallholder Farm Productivity Determines Household Food Security
anchorClaim: Increases in crop productivity among smallholder farming households in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia are associated with measurable improvements in household food security and dietary diversity, as measured in peer-reviewed agricultural economics studies.
plainQuestion: When a smallholder farming household becomes more productive or diversifies what it grows, it translates into a better, more varied diet and less hunger for the family.
confidenceSummary: The Grade D is a caution about depth: the studies use many different research methods that rarely repeat one another, and more than half were published in just the last two years, too recent to have been independently confirmed.

guide.whatScienceSays: DATOM looked at 97 studies that directly tested this claim. Of those, 93 (96%) support the idea that when a smallholder farming household grows more food or a wider variety of it, the family eats better and goes hungry less often; 4 (4%) point the other way. So most of the clear findings back the claim, which is what the "Supported" verdict below means. But the Grade D beside it matters just as much: the evidence base is limited, so this is the current direction of the evidence, not a settled, high-certainty result. Many more studies touched on the topic without testing this exact claim; they appear further down, tagged by what they looked at.
guide.howConfident:
Why 57% support doesn't mean 29% confidence: DATOM's confidence score for this claim is 29% ("Preliminary"), well below the 57% of sources that support it. That's because the confidence score measures how strong and consistent the evidence base is as a whole, not just which way the studies point.

First, the 175 sources trace back to about 93 different original studies. But they used a huge mix of methods: no single research approach accounts for more than 6 of the 175 sources, and 78 of the 175 use a method that appears only once. That makes it hard to combine these studies the way you could if they all used the same, repeated approach.

Second, 83 of the 175 sources (47%), nearly half, come from text summaries rather than the full original document. That means for almost half the evidence, we're missing some of the detail and background that a full paper would give us. As one concrete example, the sample record from Zambia's productivity program evaluation doesn't even report how many households were studied.

Third, the 41% of sources calling this "conditional" doesn't mean many studies disagree with the claim. In fact, only 4 of 175 (2%) actually disagree. What it means is that the single largest group of sources says the benefit depends on other things, like market access, local growing conditions, or women's decision-making power. That weakens our confidence that simply boosting farm productivity, on its own, would produce the same result everywhere.

DATOM also flags 25 of the underlying findings as individually too small to trust strongly on their own. That means those particular studies didn't have enough people or samples to be confident in their result by itself. That reinforces the overall picture: a lot of small, differently-designed studies rather than a few large, repeated ones.

Finally, the process that generated this claim recorded a timeout error partway through. We independently double-checked the full set of 175 sources and confirmed the counts matched, so the result is accurate. But that hiccup is one more reason to treat this score as preliminary rather than fully settled.
decisionSupport: 72 of the 175 sources (41%) say the link between farm productivity and better diets depends on things like market access, local growing conditions, or women's decision-making power. For example, one study of 768 households in southern Bangladesh found the effect gets weaker as soil salinity gets worse. So if you're designing a program, pair productivity gains with these supporting conditions rather than assuming more farm output alone will improve diets.

Only 4 of 175 sources (2%) contradict the claim, so a program that raises smallholder farm productivity is very unlikely to actively hurt household diets, even if it's not guaranteed to help in every situation.

Treat any single study's numbers as specific to its own setting: the 175 sources used 78 different one-off research methods, with no single method used more than 6 times. So no individual study's result should be treated as a stand-in for what the whole field agrees on.

47% of the sources (83 of 175) come from text summaries instead of the full original document. At least one of them, the Zambia productivity program evaluation, doesn't report how many households were included. So double-check specific numbers against the original source before citing them.

56% of this evidence (98 of 175 sources) was published in just 2025 and 2026, compared to just one source from 2011. Most of this research is very recent and hasn't yet had time to be checked or challenged by other scientists, so weigh brand-new single-country findings carefully for high-stakes decisions.
guide.faultLines:
Small, Scattered Studies: the 175 sources come from 78 different research methods that each show up only once. Even the two most common named approaches, tracking the same farm households over time with statistical modeling, and re-analyzing data from randomized trials, each account for only 6 of the 175 sources. This isn't a set of studies repeating the same test to confirm a result; it's a patchwork of one-off approaches that resist being combined into one clean answer.

Missing Details on Nearly Half the Sources: 83 of the 175 sources (47%) come from text summaries rather than the full original document. You can see the effect directly in the sample record from Zambia's smallholder productivity program evaluation, where the number of households studied is simply listed as "Not reported." This gap limits how well we can independently check the numbers behind roughly half the evidence.

Mostly Brand New Findings: 98 of the 175 sources (56%) were published in just 2025 and 2026, compared to a single source from 2011 and only a handful in any year before 2020. Most of this evidence is too new to have been retested, cited, or challenged by other researchers yet. That's a real reason to read the 57% support figure as promising but not yet fully proven.

scope: Smallholder farm households in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Central America, including Bangladesh, Ethiopia, Zambia, Uganda, Ghana, and Nicaragua.
metric: How varied and healthy people's diets are, using standard survey scores for households, children, and women (HDDS, CDDS, WDDS, HFVS), plus separate scales that measure whether a household has enough reliable access to food.
